title: U.S. Teen Mental Health Is Improving
author: Peter Gray
summary: Peter Gray presents CDC data showing that teen mental health in the United States has improved in recent years. Suicide rates for 15 to 19 year olds are on a clear downward trend after 2018, and the Youth Risk Behavior Survey shows declines in persistent sadness and suicidality between 2021 and 2025. The improvement appears among teens but not among adults, which he takes as evidence that something specific changed for young people. He recaps the argument of his book Restoring Childhood, that mental health tracks how much freedom and agency children have, that the computer revolution helped, and that Common Core made school more stressful after 2010. He notes that the CDC found no change in teens' social media use as mental health improved, which he says undercuts the smartphone explanation. His tentative theory is that parents and educators are slowly restoring independence, less pressured schooling and more outdoor play, and he invites readers to share what they observe.
points: CDC data show a sustained decline in teen suicide rates after 2018 and falling reports of sadness and suicidality between 2021 and 2025.
The improvement is concentrated in teens, since emergency visits for suspected suicide attempts fell 13.3 percent for ages 12 to 17 but barely moved for adults.
The CDC found no meaningful change in teens' social media use during the period of greatest improvement, which Gray reads as weakening the smartphone explanation.
Gray ties the long arc of teen mental health to children's freedom and agency, with Common Core and pressured schooling blamed for the post-2010 decline.
His tentative theory is that more independence, less pressured schooling and more alternative schooling are driving the recovery, and he treats it as a hypothesis for research.
quotes: This is not just a blip; it’s a significant downward trend in suicide rate. Let’s hope it continues.
Teens (ages 12-17) showed a decline of 13.3 % in such emergency visits over these years, while adults age 18-25 showed a negligible decline of 0.9% and older groups all showed increases.

Finally, in the book, I present evidence that the decline in mental health from roughly 2010 to 2018 resulted primarily from a radical, nationwide change in schooling instituted by the Common Core State Standards, which made school far less pleasant and more stressful than it had been before.

In fact, the CDC began, for the first time in 2023, to ask teens about their rate of use of social media as part of the Youth Risk Behavior Survey, and found no meaningful change in that between 2023 and 2025, a two-year period of greatest improvement in mental health, as shown in the same survey.

Call me an optimist, if you will, but I think parents and educators are gradually catching on to the idea that, for mental wellbeing (and positive development generally), kids need more time for themselves, more opportunity to do things independently, and less pressured schooling.
To be happy and mentally well, one needs some freedom. Perhaps we are, as a society, beginning to recognize that to be as true of kids as it is of the rest of us.
